h1: The 8 Best Mechanical Keyboard Layouts Explained, Ranked & Reviewed (2026)
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: eight mechanical keyboards across TKL, 75% and full-size layouts, with plain advice on which layout fits your desk and work.
summary: The AULA F75 Pro is our top pick for most people because the 75% layout keeps the function row and arrows while freeing desk space. The Logitech G413 TKL SE is the safest first step down from full-size. Spreadsheet users should look at the Keychron V6 family, and the RisoPhy and Redragon boards cover tight budgets with a numpad.
intro: The most expensive mistake in this category is buying a layout by looks. A compact board feels great in a photo, then you reach for a numpad that is no longer there, or a Home key that moved behind a function layer, and the keyboard ends up in a drawer.

We reviewed eight boards that cover the three layouts people actually choose between: tenkeyless, 75% and full-size. Each pick was ranked on layout usefulness, switch and keycap quality, connection options, and how easy it is to customize later, using the spec sheets and the experience owners report. Layout comes first because every other feature is secondary if the key you need is missing.

products.name: AULA F75 Pro Wireless Mechanical Keyboard, 75% Hot Swappable
products.verdict: A 75% board that keeps the keys you use and drops the ones you do not.
products.description:
The F75 Pro is a 75% keyboard, which means the numpad is gone and the right-hand cluster is squeezed tight, but the function row and arrow keys stay. It connects over 2.4GHz, USB-C or Bluetooth 5.0 and uses hot-swappable, pre-lubed switches under side-printed PBT keycaps.

It ranks above the Logitech G413 TKL SE because the layout is smaller and the board is wireless and swappable, so it gives back more desk without costing you navigation. The trade is a denser key arrangement than a TKL, so you will spend a few days relearning where Delete and Page Up sit.

Buy it if you move between laptop and desk and want one tidy board for both. The caveat is that anyone who enters numbers all day will miss the numpad, and a rotary knob is not a substitute for it.
products.idealFor: Hybrid workers who want a small board that still has dedicated arrow and function keys.
products.skipIf: You enter numbers or spreadsheet data for hours each day.

products.name: Logitech G413 TKL SE Mechanical Gaming Keyboard
products.verdict: The least surprising way to leave the numpad behind.
products.description:
The G413 TKL SE is a tenkeyless board, so it removes only the numpad and keeps a full function row, a dedicated arrow block and the navigation cluster. It is wired, has an aluminum-alloy top case, and works with Logitech G HUB software.

It sits just below the AULA F75 Pro because it is wired only and the switches are not hot-swappable, so there is less room to grow. What you get in return is a layout with no relearning, since every key is where a full-size board puts it.

Choose it if your priority is a smaller footprint with zero habit change. The caveat is that it does not save as much width as a 75% board, and you will not find wireless here.
products.idealFor: People moving from a full-size board who want zero relearning.
products.skipIf: You want a wireless board or plan to swap switches later.

products.name: Keychron V6 Max Wireless, Gateron Brown Switch
products.verdict: A full-size board you can finally put anywhere on the desk.
products.description:
The V6 Max with Gateron Brown switches is a full-size, wireless board running over 2.4GHz or Bluetooth 5.1. Switches are hot-swappable, the firmware is QMK/VIA, and the tactile brown switch gives a gentle bump without a loud click.

It ranks below the compact picks because full-size takes real width, and it ranks above the wired Keychron V6 because cutting the cable is worth the higher bucket for many desks. It sits just under the banana-switch version only because tactile feel suits more typists than linear does.

It suits numpad users who share a desk or want a clean cable-free setup. The caveat is the footprint, which stays large, and the price bucket is above the wired model.
products.idealFor: Numpad users who want wireless and a tactile typing feel.
products.skipIf: Desk width is tight or you prefer smooth linear switches.

products.name: Keychron V6 Max Wireless, Gateron Banana Switch
products.verdict: Same full-size wireless body, with a smooth linear stroke.
products.description:
This V6 Max uses the Gateron Banana linear switch in the same wireless full-size body: 2.4GHz and Bluetooth 5.1, hot-swappable sockets, QMK/VIA firmware and RGB backlighting.

It ranks one place below the Brown version because the layout, features and price bucket are identical, so the decision is purely switch feel. Linear switches have no tactile bump, which many typists find faster for gaming and less satisfying for long documents.

Choose it if you already know you like linear switches. The caveat is that, with hot-swap sockets, you can change your mind later, so the Brown version is not a trap either way.
products.idealFor: Typists who prefer linear switches and need a numpad.
products.skipIf: You want tactile feedback to confirm each keypress.

products.name: Keychron V6 Wired Custom Mechanical Keyboard, Knob Version
products.verdict: The tweakable full-size board without a wireless premium.
products.description:
The V6 Knob Version is a wired, full-size board with a rotary knob, hot-swappable Keychron K Pro Brown switches and open-source QMK/VIA firmware. It connects over USB-C and works with both Mac and Windows.

It lands below the Max models because it lacks wireless, but it costs a bucket less and the typing hardware is the same idea. It ranks above the plain V6 since the knob gives a fast volume dial without a function-key chord.

Buy it if the board will stay in one place and you value remapping. The caveat is the cable, and that a full-size body is still a wide piece of desk.
products.idealFor: Numpad users who like to remap keys and stay plugged in.
products.skipIf: You want to move the keyboard around without a cable.

products.name: Keychron V6 Wired, Frosted Black-Translucent
products.verdict: Keychron's hot-swap experience with the knob left off.
products.description:
This frosted V6 is a wired, full-size board with no rotary knob, hot-swappable K Pro Brown switches, QMK/VIA firmware and a frosted black-translucent case.

It ranks just under the Knob Version because the two share the same core hardware, and the only difference is a dial you may or may not use. If you never adjust volume from the keyboard, that is a fair thing to skip.

It fits shoppers who want the look of a translucent case and full remapping. The caveat is that you give up the knob and wireless in the same purchase.
products.idealFor: Buyers who want the V6 board and no extras.
products.skipIf: A volume knob or wireless matters to you.

products.name: Redragon K668 RGB Gaming Keyboard, 108 Keys
products.verdict: A budget full-size board with four extra hotkeys and swappable switches.
products.description:
The K668 is a 108-key board: the usual 104 plus four extra hotkeys. It has a hot-swappable socket fitted with a red switch, two sets of mixed-color PBT keycaps, sound-absorbing foam in the case and a wired USB connection.

It ranks below the Keychron V6 family because it has no QMK/VIA firmware, but it undercuts them on price and beats the RisoPhy for keycaps and hot-swap sockets.

It suits numpad users who want a few spare macro keys on a modest budget. The caveat is the wired-only design and a larger footprint than any compact board here.
products.idealFor: Budget shoppers who want a numpad plus extra hotkeys.
products.skipIf: You want wireless or advanced firmware remapping.

products.name: RisoPhy Mechanical Gaming Keyboard, RGB 104 Keys
products.verdict: The cheapest way to get a real numpad on a mechanical board.
products.description:
The RisoPhy is a standard 104-key full-size board with blue switches, wired USB, anti-ghosting, spill resistance, ABS keycaps and RGB backlighting.

It ranks last because switches are not hot-swappable and the keycaps are ABS, but it is the lowest price bucket here at under $50. Blue switches are clicky, so this is a board for a room of your own.

It works for someone who needs a numpad cheaply and does not mind noise. The caveat is the click, which is not friendly to shared spaces or video calls.
products.idealFor: Numpad users on a tight budget working alone.
products.skipIf: You share a room or take video calls.

methodology.title: Layout usefulness
methodology.description: We checked which keys each layout removes and whether the ones that remain cover typical work, from arrows to a numpad.

methodology.title: Desk footprint
methodology.description: Width matters on small desks, so compact layouts scored higher than full-size boards where function was equal.

methodology.title: Switch and keycap quality
methodology.description: We looked at switch type, hot-swap sockets and PBT versus ABS caps on each spec sheet.

methodology.title: Connectivity
methodology.description: Wireless and multi-device options were weighed against wired-only designs for a shared desk.

methodology.title: Customization
methodology.description: Remappable firmware and swappable switches extend a board's life, so they added to the score.

whatMatters.detail: Layout means which keys the board includes: full-size has everything, TKL drops the numpad, 75% squeezes the cluster tighter still. It matters because each cut saves desk width but removes a key you may use daily. Check the product photo for arrow keys, a function row and where Delete and Page Up sit.

A numpad is the block of digits on the right side. People who enter figures or use shortcuts built on it lose speed without it. Be honest about how often you use it, since a knob or layer does not replace it. Look for a 104 or 108 key count in the listing.

Linear switches press smoothly, tactile ones have a bump, and clicky ones add sound. The choice changes noise and feel across a full day. Check whether sockets are hot-swappable, which lets you change switches later without soldering.

Wired boards avoid battery worries, while wireless ones free the desk. Multi-mode boards pair with several devices. Look for 2.4GHz or Bluetooth in the listing, and note the cable type for wired boards.
QMK/VIA firmware lets you remap keys in software, and PBT keycaps resist shine better than ABS. Both extend ownership. Search the specs for QMK, VIA and keycap material.

cards.label: Compact
cards.text: 75% and TKL layouts save width and shorten the mouse reach. The AULA F75 Pro and Logitech G413 TKL SE lead here.

cards.label: Full-size
cards.text: Full-size keeps the numpad and extra keys, but takes more room. The Keychron V6 family, Redragon K668 and RisoPhy are the picks.

howToChoose.note: Most buyers should default to compact unless they truly use the numpad every day.

rows: Keychron V6 Max Brown, Keychron V6 Knob

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A wireless or multi-device mode, quiet tactile or linear switches, and a narrow body.

cards.label: In this ranking
cards.text: The AULA F75 Pro pairs three connection modes with a compact body. Skip the RisoPhy because of its clicky blue switches.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You want wireless full-size or long-term remapping. The Keychron V6 Max models and V6 Knob justify it through QMK/VIA firmware.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You type in one place and the numpad is the only requirement. The Redragon K668 or RisoPhy covers it.

faq.q: Is a 75% keyboard hard to get used to?
faq.a: Most people adapt within a few days. The main change is that Delete, Page Up and Page Down sit in a single compressed column. If you want no adjustment at all, the Logitech G413 TKL SE keeps standard spacing.

faq.q: What is the most common layout mistake?
faq.a: Buying a compact board and then missing the numpad or navigation keys. Count how often you use each key before you commit, because layers are slower than a real key.
It lets you change switches without soldering, so a bad first choice is not permanent. The AULA F75 Pro, Redragon K668 and Keychron V6 boards all offer it, while the Logitech and RisoPhy do not.

faq.q: Do these work on Mac and Windows?
faq.a: The Keychron V6 Knob lists Mac and Windows compatibility directly. Others generally work as standard keyboards, but confirm the keycap legends and any software support on the listing.

faq.q: How do I keep a mechanical keyboard clean?
faq.a: Pull the keycaps with a puller, brush out crumbs and wipe the plate. PBT caps resist shine, so they tend to look better longer than ABS.

faq.q: Are blue switches a problem at the office?
faq.a: Yes for shared spaces. Blue switches click audibly on every press, which is why the RisoPhy suits a private room better than an open desk.

finalTake: Start with layout, since it decides whether you will keep the board. The AULA F75 Pro is the best all-around choice, the Logitech G413 TKL SE is the safe downsize, and the Keychron V6 line serves anyone who needs a numpad and wants a board that can be remapped. The Redragon K668 and RisoPhy are fine budget answers when the numpad matters most.
